title: Bài sưu tầm 204 - Passage 2: The Vertical Agrarian Revolution in Singapore
passageHtml:
READING PASSAGE 204

The Vertical Agrarian Revolution in Singapore

Paragraph 1. Singapore represents an acute geographic paradox. With a population approaching six million people squeezed onto a landmass of barely 730 square kilometres, the island nation has historically prioritized high-density public housing, industrial ports, and commercial infrastructure over agriculture. Consequently, Singapore currently imports more than ninety percent of its total food supply from foreign trading partners, exposing the city-state to external disruptions in global transport corridors and climate-induced crop failures abroad. To insulate itself against these systemic vulnerabilities, the Singapore Food Agency formulated an ambitious national initiative known as the '30 by 30' plan. The overarching policy goal is to produce thirty percent of the nation’s nutritional requirements locally by the year 2030, using less than one percent of the country’s total land area.

Paragraph 2. To accomplish this goal without compromising scarce residential and industrial zoning, local agrarian enterprises are abandoning traditional soil cultivation in favour of indoor vertical hydroponics. Leading this technological transition is GroFarm, an agrotechnology company operating within a converted multi-storey logistics warehouse in northern Singapore. GroFarm’s facility utilizes an automated rotating vertical carousel system spanning nine vertical metres. Seedlings of leafy greens—such as bok choy, kale, and Chinese spinach—are nested inside shallow plastic troughs bathed in a constantly circulating nutrient solution consisting of recycled water, potassium, nitrogen, and essential minerals. By replacing natural soil with an aqueous delivery system, the closed-loop design slashes water consumption by ninety-five percent compared to conventional open-field farming.

Paragraph 3. The primary operational advantage of vertical indoor cultivation is absolute environmental insulation. Inside GroFarm’s facility, atmospheric humidity, ambient temperature, and carbon dioxide concentrations are continuously governed by computerized sensors. High-efficiency light-emitting diode (LED) arrays emit specialized wavelengths of blue and deep red photons optimized for photosynthesis, eliminating the crop's dependence on unpredictable natural sunlight. Because the growth environment is hermetically sealed against the outside world, insect pests and soil-borne bacterial pathogens cannot penetrate the facility. As a result, GroFarm produces crops completely free of synthetic pesticides, achieving up to twelve harvest cycles per year compared to the four cycles typical of regional outdoor agricultural plots.

Paragraph 4. However, the vertical farming model faces persistent economic skepticism, primarily centering on energetic expenditures. While traditional rural agriculture utilizes free solar radiation, indoor vertical facilities consume colossal amounts of electricity to power thousands of high-intensity LED panels and industrial air-conditioning systems required to dissipate excess heat generated by lighting fixtures. In Singapore, where national power generation relies overwhelmingly on imported liquefied natural gas, high electricity tariffs can account for up to forty percent of an indoor farm's total operating budget. Consequently, locally grown hydroponic vegetables typically command a retail price fifteen to twenty percent higher than field-grown produce imported from neighbouring Malaysia or Thailand.

Paragraph 5. To bridge this economic gap, agronomists are exploring biological and structural efficiencies. Researchers at the Singapore Institute of Food Innovation are selectively breeding dwarfed, fast-maturing vegetable cultivars tailored specifically to high-density artificial light. Concurrently, engineers are experimenting with integrating rooftop solar arrays and waste-heat recovery pumps to reduce net grid dependence. Moreover, the Singaporean government has introduced supportive procurement subsidies, requiring public hospitals, schools, and military establishments to source a minimum quota of fresh greens from domestic vertical suppliers. Whether high-tech indoor agronomy can truly achieve self-sustaining economic parity remains uncertain, but Singapore’s vertical farms provide the world with an essential testing ground for urban resilience in an increasingly volatile climate.

q14.text: Singapore currently relies on foreign nations for the vast majority of its domestic food supply.

steps: Đoạn 1: "...currently imports more than ninety percent of its total food supply..." → vast majority.

q15.text: The '30 by 30' plan requires agricultural enterprises to acquire large portions of residential land.

steps: Đoạn 1 & 2: "...using less than one percent of the country’s total land area... without compromising scarce residential and industrial zoning..." → Mâu thuẫn trực tiếp với acquire large portions.

q16.text: GroFarm was established inside a building that was originally used for storage and logistics.

steps: Đoạn 2: "...operating within a converted multi-storey logistics warehouse..." → warehouse = storage and logistics.

q17.text: GroFarm’s vegetables require smaller amounts of synthetic chemical fertilizer than traditional crops.

steps: Đoạn 2 & 3: Có nhắc đến nutrient solution và free of synthetic pesticides, nhưng hoàn toàn không có dữ liệu so sánh lượng phân bón (fertilizer) giữa phương pháp này với phương pháp truyền thống.

q18.text: Produce grown in Singaporean vertical farms is currently cheaper in grocery stores than imported vegetables.

steps: Đoạn 4: "...hydroponic vegetables typically command a retail price fifteen to twenty percent higher than field-grown produce imported..." → Đắt hơn chứ không phải rẻ hơn.
Đoạn 3: "...emit specialized wavelengths of blue and deep red photons..."
Đoạn 3: "...produces crops completely free of synthetic pesticides..."
Đoạn 4: "...high electricity tariffs can account for up to forty percent..." (Distractor: gas).
